TESTIMONY OF ALICIA REA LD 16 - Ought Not To Pass
An Act to Establish Separate Prosecutorial Districts in Downeast Maine
JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON JUDICIARY
January 22, 2025
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn and distinguished members of the
Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary, greetings. My name is Alicia Rea, and I am a policy fellow at the American Civil Liberties Union of Maine, a
statewide organization committed to advancing and preserving civil
liberties guaranteed by the Maine and U.S. Constitutions. On behalf of our
members, I respectfully urge you to oppose this bill.
A culture of punishment, combined with race- and class-based
discrimination, has led the United States to rely on incarceration more heavily than any other country in the world -- and our society is no safer for it. The politicization of criminal legal policy and a lack of evidence-based assessment result in a one-way street in which law and policy grow ever
more punitive. The human and financial costs of mass incarceration are
staggering, and the burden falls disproportionately on the poor and people
of color.
Prosecutors remain the most influential actors in the criminal legal system.
The discretion to make charging decisions and plea offers continues to
influence incarceration rates, implicating racially disparate impacts on detention and incarceration. Prosecutorial discretion with little judicial oversight has led to an inequitable system that continues to pour resources into incarcerating Mainers.
The ACLU of Maine understands that having a separate elected district
attorney in Washington County could potentially lead to better, more individualized decisions concerning the criminal legal system. Because this district attorney would be selected by Washington County voters, they might be more aware of the devastating effects that the criminalization of poverty and health conditions like substance use disorder have had on the

those practices. However, establishing a new prosecutorial district expands the criminal legal system. It would instead be best to examine how we can shrink the criminal legal system, reduce mass incarceration, and pursue
proven solutions that improve public safety. Evidence-based solutions address the root causes of social issues like homelessness and substance use by meeting people's basic needs of affordable housing, health care, education, and job training.
In addition, we would note that Maine already has eight district attorney offices and an Attorney General's office, yet the state has only four public
defender offices. For example, Prosecutorial District 3 covers Androscoggin,
Franklin, and Oxford counties. Each of these counties has different needs of their prosecutors for covering the settings -- from the more populous city of Lewiston to the rural town of Kingfield. While addressing an imbalance in current prosecutorial resources is beyond the scope of this legislation, we felt compelled to remind the committee of it in connection with its
deliberation.
Thank you for your time and attention.
10031382:
Amanda Anderson Trescott LD 16
I am disappointed to see this mis-guided proposal brought forward again. I am happy to be able to say that District Attorney Bob Granger is professional, capable, and effective, and I do not believe that Washington County is ill-served by his administration. I see this move to establish a separate Washington County district as founded in a desire among a short list of parties influential within the county to effectively secede Washington County from the governance of the State of Maine, by bringing control of the judiciary within reach of their influence. They could then see the laws enforced according to their preferences, and citizens of Washington County would find themselves living in a backward fiefdom governed wholly by the undue influence of a small group of well-connected individuals. Crony capitalism unchecked, in other words. We recently had a very public example of this line of thinking with the "Freedom Flagpole" development plan, slated for Columbia Falls, where the developer brought a proposal before the Legislature that his property should be annexed by the neighboring town. He stated outright that he wanted to pull the land from an unorganized town, under LUPC jurisdiction, into the neighboring organized town, under DEP jurisdiction, because the environmental regulations are more relaxed under DEP! The Legislature approved, the Governor signed on, and shortly afterward, we learned of a recently built development of several cabins on another parcel in his ownership where no notification or application to DEP had been made at all. The DEP visited the site, and found major violations of the regs. He refused to engage in site remediation measures they ordered, and they enforced fines. The "Freedom Flagpole" development effort has since imploded altogether, failing to attract needed financing, and as of last summer, he was still paying fines on the cabin development. I hope that the Legislature and Governor will take a lesson from this experience, and will not be approving such mis-guided, self-interested proposals. If there are any questions regarding these comments, please post them to my e-mail address. I check this regularly, and can respond promptly. Thank you for your consideration.

L.D. 16 An Act To Establish Separate Prosecutorial Districts in Downeast Maine

Dear Committee Members and Respective Chairs:

Good Morning - my name is Barry Curtis, Sheriff of Washington County. Before being elected in 2014, I served the Maine State Police for 25 years as a Trooper. The last 15 years of my career, I moved home to serve the citizens of Troop J, which covers Washington and Hancock Counties. After being elected in 2014 I realized things had changed in law enforcement and I had only taken a four-year break. The types of crimes changed, the frequency of crime changed and the demands of law enforcement had changed. Since law enforcement officer's caseloads become the caseloads of the District Attorney's Office, these changes have also greatly impacted them.

Around 1975 District Attorney's Offices replaced County Attorneys and at this time counties were combined to form the current Prosecution Districts. Since 1975 Washington County has shared a District Attorney with Hancock County. In the last 45 years there have only been three District Attorneys elected and all three have been from Hancock County. As a matter of fact, one individual moved from Washington County to Hancock County before running for the office.

Washington County is a relatively large county, in excess of 3000 square miles, which is over twice the size of the State of Rhode Island but has the population of the city of

www.washingtoncountymaine.com

Bangor. Our county has two District Attorney's Offices and two courthouses; one in Machias and the other in Calais, 33 miles apart. Historically, as well as currently, the District Attorney has their office in Ellsworth which means he or she will travel to Washington County when necessary. The District Attorney's office in Ellsworth is 57 miles away from the office in Machias and 91 miles away from the office in Calais.
Washington County use to have Assistant District Attorneys as well as Deputy District Attorneys that lived and worked in Washington County. This has not been the case in recent years as we have gone from three full time Assistant District Attorneys to one full time and one-part time. It is my understanding there are open positions, but filling them has proven to be quite difficult. Hancock County currently has three Assistant District Attorneys plus the District Attorney to handle the caseloads for that county.
Over the last five years, in my position as Sheriff, I have seen a decline in the number of cases being prosecuted. It seems more and more cases are plead down or just dismissed. I feel this is a direct correlation to the caseload and lack of personnel in Washington County. I understand the difficulties in running and managing offices so far away from one another, while still working on caseloads, and running the office in Hancock County and working so shorthanded.
I want to be clear, when I say, this is not about our current District Attorney, this is about the position of District Attorney. These issues will be present regardless of the person in the office as long as they live in Hancock County. I would suspect similar issues if the District Attorney lived and worked mostly in Washington County. Too that point, the population of Hancock County is 55,497 compared to Washington County's 31,595. Therefore, I don't foresee a District Attorney being elected from Washington County. If the citizens of Washington County are unhappy with the job I am doing as their Sheriff, they have the option of electing a new Sheriff. I am not sure this is the case with the District Attorney as long as the position encompasses both Washington and Hancock counties.
It is my opinion the citizens of Washington County would greatly benefit from having our own District Attorney. Having a District Attorney, dedicated to the people of Washington County would allow better management of the offices, caseloads as well as allow more time to work hand in hand with Law Enforcement. Thus providing a better service to the citizens of Washington County and quite frankly the citizens of Hancock County as well.
Thank you for your time today, it is greatly appreciated.

10031325:
Kiernan Majerus-Collins Auburn, Maine LD 16
I ask the Committee to oppose LD 16 because it unnecessarily costs the state money and because it reduces democratic accountability in the form of competitive elections. LD 16 would create the two smallest prosecutorial districts by population in the state, and would create a precedent that could lead to the creation of many additional prosecutorial districts that would still be larger than the proposed District 9 in LD 16. Maine's eight district attorneys could easily become twelve or more based on the logic of LD 16; after all, if Washington County's 32,000 residents need their own district attorney, wouldn't the same hold true for Oxford County's 59,000, Waldo County's 41,000, Sagadahoc County's 38,000, and Lincoln County's 37,000?
In addition to extra costs associated with more elected prosecutors and additional bureaucracy, shrinking the size of prosecutorial districts would further undermine efforts to hold these powerful officials accountable. Legislative oversight efforts would be stretched, as would investigative journalism efforts. Perhaps worst of all, creating additional offices would only increase the likelihood that candidates would run unopposed, thereby depriving voters of any meaningful input as to who serves as their local district attorney. Rural Maine has a hard enough time finding lawyers who are willing to run for and serve in these important offices; increasing the number of elected prosecutors will only result in more uncontested elections. Please vote no on this likely well-intentioned, but ultimately counterproductive bill.

Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary,
We, the undersigned legislators representing most of Hancock County, are writing to express our support for Senator Marianne Moore's LD 16, An Act To Establish Separate Prosecutorial Districts in Downeast Maine. This proposed legislation is a critical step toward ensuring fair and effective administration of justice for the residents of
both counties.
Hancock and Washington Counties are vastly different in terms of demographics, resources, and challenges, making it increasingly difficult to manage them as a single prosecutorial district. Hancock County has nearly double the population of Washington County, with a median household income exceeding $72,000. In contrast, Washington County, while geographically larger, has a median household income of just over $50,000. These economic and demographic disparities reflect some of the distinct challenges each county faces.
Hancock County benefits from greater access to resources and infrastructure, while Washington County's rural and expansive geography poses unique challenges in delivering services effectively. These differences underscore the need for tailored prosecutorial approaches that address the specific needs of each county.
The strain on the prosecutor's office in this combined district has become increasingly evident in recent years. The current arrangement spreads prosecutorial resources thin, making it challenging to provide timely and focused attention to cases in both counties. Dividing the district would alleviate this burden and allow for a more efficient allocation of resources. Each county would benefit from having a dedicated prosecutor who can address its unique legal and community needs.
We believe that separating the prosecutorial districts will improve the quality ofjustice, enhance community trust
in the legal system, and ensure that residents in both Hancock and Washington Counties receive the focused
attention they desenle.
We urge you to vote to pass LD 16. This change is not only logical but necessary to address the evolving and
distinct needs of our counties.
Thank you for considering this important matter. We are committed to working together to advance this legislation
and to ensure that justice is equitably and efficiently served.
Sincerely,

Public Testimony of LD 16 - An Act to Establish Separate Prosecutorial Districts in Downeast Maine
Presented by Representative Strout of Harrington - District 11
Good afternoon, Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn and distinguished members of the Judiciary committee. I am Representative Tiffany Strout from Harrington, representing the towns of Milbridge, Harrington, Columbia, Columbia Falls, Centerville, Addison, Jonesport, Beals, Jonesboro, Roque Bluffs, Whitneyville and Machias and I am here today to provide testimony in support of LD 16 An Act to Establish Separate Prosecutorial Districts in DownEast Maine.
Growing up in DownEast Maine was a wonderful opportunity to be with generations of family and for the close-knit communities. In addition, the area was always safe and crime was low especially violent crime. I grew up in the no cell phone age, not the dark age like my kid thinks, but in a time where we would leave the house and be told what time to be home and there was no worry in between.
Unfortunately, the days of how I grew up seem to be falling further away. I attribute the increase in crime to both mental health decline as well as the drug epidemic we have in our county. The increase in these problems has escalated crime and the need for speedy processing of those accused of the crimes to levels that were not experienced even 10 years ago.
Our current District Attorney, Mr. Granger, who we share with Hancock County, has brought back integrity and due process to the District Attorney's offices. This bill is not intended to take away from the impact and good work he and his team have and will continue to provide, this bills intent is to free up his time to focus on a single county case load for more efficient case review and prosecution.
I think we all wish we wouldn't have to have the conversation about adding any additional District Attorneys or Law Enforcement to the state, but unfortunately, that is not the time we are currently living in. Instead, we are at a point where people are struggling and making tough decisions, sometimes resulting in breaking the laws. Allowing Washington County to have their own District Attorney works toward the due process as outlined in the 4th, 5th, 6th, 8th and 14th amendments.
Those charged with a crime have the right to an attorney and a speedy trial. To keep with those promises the Constitution outlines, Washington County should have their own District Attorney allowing timely thorough investigations to help insure those innocent are not wrongfully convicted and those who should be convicted do not have their charges dismissed for lack of Constitutional guarantees.
Thank you for your time today and I would be glad to answer any questions.
Sincerely,
Tiffany Strout State Representative

Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, Distinguished Members of the Judiciary
Committee:
My name is Will Tuell, and I represent House District 10 which includes nearly
two dozen towns and unorganized townships in central Washington County.
I am here today in strong support of LD 16, which, as the title indicates, would
establish separate prosecutorial districts in Hancock and Washington counties, sponsored by Sen. Moore and a bi-partisan, bi-county coalition of lawmakers on
behalf of law enforcement, attorneys, and communities in Down East Maine.
This is not my first rodeo pushing for this legislation. As your analyst can attest, I
have presented similar legislation twice before in the 129"` and 130"` legislatures - first to hold a referendum of both counties' voters and secondly to split the
district straight up.
There will be a lot of talk today about the numbers, caseloads, and cost to the
counties involved. And before I go any further, l want to credit our current district attorney, Bob Granger, for engaging in an open and honest dialogue. It has only
helped us better prepare our case, and is, in the interest of transparency,
commendable. Mr. Granger is a hardworking attorney who cares for the people he represents, and while we disagree, I admire him for putting himself out there.
That being said, my reasoning for supporting this legislation is as it always has
been: equal representation.
While the DA position is a law enforcement position it is also a political position
much like yours and mine are. We sen/e at the sufferance of our constituents.
Each of our districts are different; some of us have one big town or city, others have one big community and a few small surrounding communities, while others have too many to count, and they're spread out over a tvvo-and-a-half hour drive.
The one thing we all have in common though is our districts change every ten
years based on population. I used to represent the Machias area plus Lubec and Eastport, and because I lived in the Machias area and it accounted for the most
population, my constituents there probably got better representation than those
who live, say, in Eastport. No fault of mine or yours if you find yourself in a similar situation. lt's just the reality, and the only way of evening it out is to redistrict
every ten years as populations shift.

House District 10

At the same time, counties elect our own sheriff, treasurer, Register of Deeds
and Probate, as well as our own Probate Judge. We do not share these offices
with other counties, and the people of the county have the sole say who fills that
particular office.
Yet, in the forty plus years since Washington and Hancock counties have "shared" a DA, Washington County has not once elected the person filling that seat, and likely never will since Hancock County's population is nearly twice that of Washington County.
While it may not have been that way in the beginning, it is only getting harder for people in East Machias or Pembroke or Cooper to have a say in who their top prosecutor is. Unlike our positions where retail politics is critical, many have
never, and will never meet their DA in the grocery store.
instead of our sheriff walking next door and having a conversation with the DA,
he or his staff (or the DA) has to travel to meet them somewhere. The same is
true with defense attorneys and other stakeholders in the judicial system.
Yes, there is a DA office in Machias, and the people there do good work, but it is not the same thing as having "the DA" close by, and doesn't lend itself to
spontaneous conversations that can open the door to getting something done.
Washington County has a diverse population with specific needs, whether we are
talking about the Native American population as Rep. Dana can attest or the
Hispanic population living in Rep. Strout's district, or those grappling with drug
abuse or mental health issues.
For all of our challenges, and our small, scattered population, Washington County truly is a' place unlike any other.
To underscore that point, I would remind the committee that Aroostook County
has its own DA despite having a small, scattered, rural population. Why?
Because, like Washington, it is spread out geographically and can not be
effectively represented othen/vise.
That is why I join you today and urge you to pass LD 16. In closing, I want to
thank our cosponsors from Hancock County forjoining us in this legislation, for listening, hearing us out, and realizing that it is for the best for both counties and for the state as a whole.
Thank you,
Rep. Will Tuell
